concepts.decision: Select maintained language/runtime versions with security support and an accountable upgrade plan.
concepts.definition: Languages and supported versions chosen for maintainability, secure features, tool support, and known lifecycle ownership.
concepts.failureExample: A team can write careful code yet inherit risk from an unsupported runtime with no security fixes.
concepts.label: Programming Languages

concepts.decision: Choose maintained, reviewed libraries with known provenance, licensing, version constraints, and vulnerability response ownership.
concepts.definition: Reusable code components and frameworks included in an application to supply functions or security-relevant behavior.
concepts.failureExample: Copying an unvetted package or stale library can import an exploitable dependency into every build.
concepts.label: Libraries

concepts.decision: Harden and manage IDEs/extensions, keep them updated, and prevent privileged credentials or unreviewed plugins from widening the workstation attack surface.
concepts.definition: An integrated development environment and its extensions, settings, credentials, and plugins used to create and maintain code.
concepts.failureExample: A malicious IDE extension can read source and developer tokens before code ever reaches the repository.
concepts.label: Ide

concepts.decision: Require authenticated changes, protected critical branches, review/approval rules, and traceable links from change to revision.
concepts.definition: A system that records controlled versions, branches, changes, authorship, and merge history for source and related artifacts.
concepts.failureExample: Direct unreviewed pushes to the release branch can introduce a backdoor with no accountable review.
concepts.label: Source Control

concepts.decision: Keep secrets out of code/logs, use scoped identities to retrieve them, rotate on exposure or lifecycle events, and record references rather than values.
concepts.definition: Controlled storage, retrieval, rotation, revocation, and audit of credentials, keys, tokens, and other sensitive values.
concepts.failureExample: A production token in a repository can be cloned, cached, and reused long after the code change is removed.
concepts.label: Secrets Management

concepts.decision: Apply least privilege, review rules, protected release paths, backup/availability, and alerting for sensitive changes.
concepts.definition: Protection of source/artifact repositories through access control, branch protection, review, integrity, availability, and audit.
concepts.failureExample: A repository administrator’s unmonitored account can alter both source history and release configuration.
concepts.label: Repository Security

concepts.decision: Use strong authentication, least privilege, separate personal/organizational and environment identities, and timely revocation.
concepts.definition: An attributable, managed identity used by a developer or automation to access development resources with defined privileges.
concepts.failureExample: Shared developer accounts erase accountability and make compromise containment uncertain.
concepts.label: Developer Identity

misconceptions.claim: Deleting a secret from the current branch removes exposure.
misconceptions.correction: History, forks, caches, logs, and build artifacts may retain it; revoke and rotate first, then clean and monitor.

outcome: Apply access, isolation, inventory, and secret controls to the development environment.

sections.body: Select supported languages and libraries with maintained versions, secure defaults, inventory, license and vulnerability review, and clear ownership. Harden IDEs and developer endpoints, require strong identity and least privilege, separate personal and organizational credentials, and protect repository branches and reviews.
keyPoints: Language and library choice changes vulnerability and maintenance exposure.
IDE plugins and local tooling can read source and secrets.
Repository permissions and review protect source integrity but do not prove build integrity.
sections.title: Control people, languages, libraries, and IDEs

sections.body: Store secrets in managed systems, scope and rotate them, prevent leakage in code and logs, and use separate credentials per environment. Document runtime versions, configuration, dependencies, and service identity so deployment behavior is reproducible and drift is detectable.
keyPoints: A secret in source control remains exposed even after deletion from the latest commit.
Runtime and configuration drift can invalidate test assumptions.
Short-lived, scoped credentials reduce blast radius.
sections.title: Keep secrets and runtime assumptions bounded
